title: The Great Star: The Cullinan Diamond from Pit to Sceptre
subtitle: Premier mine, Pretoria; Transvaal Legislative Assembly; Sandringham; Amsterdam; 1905–1911, with a modern coda
intro: Late on a January afternoon in 1905, on his round of the Premier mine's open pit near Pretoria, the surface manager Frederick Wells saw something bright in the wall and cut it out with a pocket-knife. It was a diamond of about 3,106 metric carats, more than three times the size of any found before. It took the name of the company chairman, Thomas Cullinan. Within three years it had been bought by the colony, given to the King, split in Amsterdam, and set in the regalia of the British Crown.

Almost none of the record is diaries. This chapter is built from what does survive: company papers and later family recollections, the Johannesburg press, the geologists' printed description, the printed debates of the Transvaal Legislative Assembly, the private letters of politicians and the Governor (known through Bill Guest's archival study), Colonial Office telegrams, the press cables that carried the story across the Empire, the Asscher firm's photographs, and the Royal Collection's records of where the stones were set. Forms are tagged honestly; legends are marked as legends.

The stone's politics are the heart of the matter. In August 1907, five years after the end of the South African War, Louis Botha's Het Volk government asked the depressed colony to pay £150,000 for it as a birthday gift to Edward VII. Afrikaner generals spoke for it, one of them admitting he could not yet call himself loyal. Labour voted with the government. The English-speaking Progressives voted against, in public on grounds of hardship and in private calling it a bribe. The vote was 42 to 19.

The men who dug the stone are the hardest to see. The Premier pit was worked by Black African labourers, among them several hundred men recruited from Nyasaland in 1906. Recruiting there was stopped because so many died. No firsthand account by any of them has been found, and the worker who in some accounts first saw the stone is not named in any source consulted. The chapter gives them an eye of their own, built from the official records that counted them.

The coda follows the stones into the Sceptre and the Imperial State Crown in 1909–10. It ends with the calls since 2022 for their return to South Africa. Those calls, and the answer that the stone was bought and given by an elected colonial government, are set out as positions.
calendar_note: All dates are Gregorian. Weights need care: period reports give the rough as 3,025¾ carats in the old English carat (about 205 mg) and the Asscher firm worked in Dutch carats. The metric carat of 200 mg, adopted internationally from about 1907–1914, gives the familiar 3,106 ct; L. J. Spencer discussed the discrepancy in the Mineralogical Magazine in 1910. Cut-stone weights here (530.2, 317.4 ct) are metric.

eyes.name: Frederick G. S. Wells
eyes.role: Surface manager (in some accounts 'mine manager' or overseer) of the Premier (Transvaal) Diamond Mining Company, 1905
eyes.side: Premier mine management; British colonial Transvaal
eyes.vantage_label: the manager who drew the stone from the pit wall
eyes.form: statements reported in the press (1905) and a family recollection (written later, 1946)
eyes.authenticity: No diary by Wells is known. The find is recorded in company papers, the 1905 press and the Hatch and Corstorphine description; the most vivid detail comes from his daughter's magazine account of 1946, a later family recollection. Accounts differ on whether an African worker first pointed out the stone and on the date (25 or 26 January).
eyes.bio: Wells was making the evening round of the open pit when he saw a bright object in the side wall and cut it out with a pocket-knife. The company is reported to have paid him a reward. His angle is that of the white supervisor to whom the find is credited; the men who worked the face under him left no account.

sources.title: Heritage Portal: The Cullinan Diamond and other remarkable stones from the Premier / Cullinan Mine
K. Scarratt and R. Shor, 'The Cullinan Diamond Centennial', Gems & Gemology 42(2), 2006

eyes.name: Sir Thomas Major Cullinan
eyes.role: Chairman of the Premier (Transvaal) Diamond Mining Company, aged 42 in 1905; from 1907 member of the Transvaal Legislative Assembly for Pretoria North-West
eyes.side: Premier company; Transvaal National Association; friend of Botha and Smuts
eyes.where: Johannesburg and Pretoria; the mine at Elandsfontein
eyes.vantage_label: the owner whose name the stone took
eyes.form: company records; biography based on family papers (written later, 1974)
eyes.authenticity: Cullinan left no published diary. His part is known from company records and correspondence used by his grandson Nigel Helme in Thomas Major Cullinan: A Biography (1974), and from the Premier company's dealings reported in the press. Helme's account, written long after, is the source of the statement that an African worker led Wells to the stone.
eyes.bio: A builder and prospector who bought the Elandsfontein farm in 1902 and opened the Premier mine in 1903, Cullinan saw the stone the day after the find and gave it his name. He then had to sell a gem too large for any buyer, and sat in the Assembly that voted to buy it for the King.

sources.title: K. Scarratt and R. Shor, 'The Cullinan Diamond Centennial', Gems & Gemology 42(2), 2006
Heritage Portal: The Cullinan Diamond and other remarkable stones from the Premier / Cullinan Mine
B. Guest, 'The "Row about the Great Diamond": The Presentation of the Cullinan Diamond to the British Crown, 1907', Historia 52(2), 2007

eyes.name: African mineworkers at the Premier mine (collective)
eyes.role: Black African labourers who dug and sorted the kimberlite, among them recruits from Nyasaland (now Malawi) brought in under official sanction in 1906
eyes.side: African migrant and local workers under the Transvaal labour system
eyes.where: Premier mine and its compounds; homes across southern and central Africa
eyes.vantage_label: on the face; recorded only by others
eyes.form: official returns and parliamentary answers (records by others); no surviving firsthand account found
eyes.authenticity: No surviving firsthand account found. The worker who in some accounts pointed out the stone is unnamed in every source consulted; Guest (2007) calls him an unnamed Black labourer. What survives is official: Colonial Office returns of recruits and their mortality, answered in Parliament in 1908.
eyes.bio: The stone came out of a pit worked by thousands of African men on contracts. The record names the white surface manager, the chairman and the cutters, but none of the men on the shift. A Colonial Office return gives one hard figure: 463 Nyasaland recruits on the Premier mine by the end of July 1907, with recruiting halted over deaths.

sources.title: Hansard, HC Deb 11 March 1908, 'Natives in the South African Mines'
B. Guest, 'The "Row about the Great Diamond": The Presentation of the Cullinan Diamond to the British Crown, 1907', Historia 52(2), 2007

eyes.name: The Transvaal Leader (Johannesburg), unsigned writers
eyes.vantage_label: the city press that put the stone on show
eyes.authenticity: Issues of February 1905 are cited by Scarratt and Shor (2006) and Guest (2007); the paper itself was not consulted directly for this chapter.
eyes.bio: The Leader reported the crowds that queued at the Standard Bank to see the stone and proposed that the Empire's subjects buy it for the King by public subscription. Its idea of a gift was British and voluntary; the gift that came two years later was the Boer government's, paid from public funds.

sources.title: K. Scarratt and R. Shor, 'The Cullinan Diamond Centennial', Gems & Gemology 42(2), 2006
B. Guest, 'The "Row about the Great Diamond": The Presentation of the Cullinan Diamond to the British Crown, 1907', Historia 52(2), 2007

eyes.name: Frederick Henry Hatch (with George Steuart Corstorphine)
eyes.role: Mining engineer and geologist in Johannesburg; with Corstorphine, author of the first technical description of the stone
eyes.authenticity: The description appeared as a pamphlet in April 1905, in the Geological Magazine (1905) and in the Transactions of the Geological Society of South Africa vol. 8 (1906), from a lecture of March 1905. Cited from the GIA reading list and the Heritage Portal; the texts were not read in full here.
eyes.bio: Hatch and Corstorphine handled and measured the crystal within weeks of the find and described its faces and cleavage surfaces. Their account is the nearest thing to an assay report on the rough. It gives 25 January as the date of the find, against the company's 26 January.

sources.title: GIA, Cullinan Diamond reading list (period sources)
Heritage Portal: The Cullinan Diamond and other remarkable stones from the Premier / Cullinan Mine

eyes.name: Louis Botha
eyes.role: Former Boer commander-in-chief; Prime Minister of the self-governing Transvaal from March 1907, leader of Het Volk
eyes.vantage_label: the prime minister who proposed the gift
eyes.form: parliamentary speech (printed debates) and dated letters
eyes.authenticity: His motion and speech of 19 August 1907 are printed in the Transvaal Legislative Assembly Debates, vol. 1, cols 2505–2508; his private letter to Selborne of 15 August 1907 is in the Selborne Papers, Bodleian Library (Ms 60). Both are cited from Guest (2007).
eyes.bio: Five years after the war ended, Botha asked a hard-up colony to buy the stone and give it to the King. Supporters read it as a gesture of reconciliation; opponents as a party move or a bribe for a loan. His own words in the Assembly framed it as a gracious act above narrow interest.

sources.title: B. Guest, 'The "Row about the Great Diamond": The Presentation of the Cullinan Diamond to the British Crown, 1907', Historia 52(2), 2007

eyes.name: Sir (James) Percy FitzPatrick
eyes.role: Rand mining-house figure, author of Jock of the Bushveld; Progressive member for Pretoria South Central
eyes.vantage_label: the opposition member who voted no
eyes.authenticity: His speech is in the Assembly Debates (cols 2518–2520, 19 August 1907); his letter to his son of 20 August 1907 is in the FitzPatrick Papers, National English Literary Museum (A/L 4), cited from Guest (2007). The letter is unpublished, so it is digested here without quotation.
eyes.bio: FitzPatrick voted with Sir George Farrar's Progressives against the purchase. In public he defended his party's loyalty in a subdued speech; in private he gave his son five reasons, among them that the gift was a bribe to British opinion and a trap that used the King's name.

sources.title: B. Guest, 'The "Row about the Great Diamond": The Presentation of the Cullinan Diamond to the British Crown, 1907', Historia 52(2), 2007

eyes.name: Jacobus Herculaas (Koos) de la Rey
eyes.role: Former Boer general; member of the Transvaal Legislative Assembly (Het Volk)
eyes.where: Pretoria, Legislative Assembly; home district Lichtenburg
eyes.vantage_label: the Boer general who would not pretend
eyes.authenticity: Speech in the Assembly Debates, cols 2514–2515, 19 August 1907, digested from Guest (2007).
eyes.bio: De la Rey backed the gift but told the Assembly plainly that he could not yet profess loyalty to the Crown; that feeling would have to grow. He gives the Afrikaner case for the gift without the language of loyalty that its British supporters wanted to hear.

sources.title: B. Guest, 'The "Row about the Great Diamond": The Presentation of the Cullinan Diamond to the British Crown, 1907', Historia 52(2), 2007

eyes.name: William Waldegrave Palmer, 2nd Earl of Selborne
eyes.role: High Commissioner for South Africa and Governor of the Transvaal, 1905–1910
eyes.vantage_label: the governor between the parties and the King
eyes.authenticity: Letters to Farrar (15 Aug 1907), to the King's secretary Lord Knollys (20 Aug), to Churchill (telegram, 22 Aug) and to Lord Elgin (26 Aug) survive in the Selborne Papers (Bodleian) and the Colonial Office Confidential Print (CO 879/94, 879/106); cited from Guest (2007), not read in the original.
eyes.bio: Selborne urged London to accept, reading Botha's offer as a sign that Afrikaners accepted British rule. He refused to lean on the Progressives and asked the King to recognise their honest, if mistaken, sense of duty. The King did not take that advice.

sources.title: B. Guest, 'The "Row about the Great Diamond": The Presentation of the Cullinan Diamond to the British Crown, 1907', Historia 52(2), 2007

eyes.name: Winston Spencer Churchill
eyes.role: Parliamentary Under-Secretary of State for the Colonies, 1905–1908, aged 32–33
eyes.vantage_label: the minister who answered for the mines
eyes.form: correspondence received (Churchill Archive) and parliamentary answers (Hansard)
eyes.authenticity: Hopwood's letter to Churchill of 27 September 1907 is CHAR 2/30/84 at the Churchill Archives Centre; Selborne's telegram of 22 August 1907 is in the Selborne Papers. His answers of 11 March 1908 are in Hansard. The often-told story that Churchill persuaded the King to accept rests on later accounts and is not shown by these documents.
eyes.bio: Churchill's papers hold the news of the King's acceptance, and in Parliament he answered for the African recruits on the same mine. The two records rarely meet: the diamond in one file, the 463 Nyasaland men and the halt to recruiting in another.

sources.title: Churchill Archives Centre, CHAR 2/30/84 (Hopwood to Churchill, 27 Sep 1907)
Hansard, HC Deb 11 March 1908, 'Natives in the South African Mines'

eyes.name: Edward VII and the Royal Household
eyes.role: King of the United Kingdom; acting through his secretary Lord Knollys and the Colonial Secretary Lord Elgin. From May 1910 the Household records continue under George V
eyes.form: official messages (through ministers), Household letters and Royal Collection records
eyes.authenticity: The King's acceptance survives in Colonial Office telegrams and in the cabled text printed by the press on 11–13 November 1907; Knollys's letter to Selborne of 20 Sept 1907 is in the Selborne Papers. Settings of the stones are recorded by the Royal Collection Trust. The King's private diary was not consulted.
eyes.bio: Advised by his ministers, the King accepted the stone as a sign of loyalty from the whole colony, not one party, and kept it among the Crown's heirlooms. He received the two great cut stones a year later; Cullinan I went into the Sovereign's Sceptre in 1910, after his death.

sources.title: Royal Collection Trust, The Sovereign's Sceptre with Cross (RCIN 31712)
Royal Collection Trust, The Imperial State Crown (RCIN 31701)

eyes.name: Joseph Asscher (I. J. Asscher & Co., Amsterdam)
eyes.role: Head cleaver of the Asscher diamond-cutting firm, Tolstraat, Amsterdam
eyes.vantage_label: the hand that struck the blade
eyes.form: firm's photographs and records; statements reported in the press (1908)
eyes.authenticity: The firm's photograph album 'The Cullinan, by Joseph Asscher & Cie' is in the Royal Collection. Press cables of February 1908 and a 1909 survey describe the cleaving; a 1908 Jewelers' Circular Weekly piece gives his brother Louis's account. The story that Joseph fainted after the blow is a later legend; the family denied it.
eyes.bio: Asscher spent days cutting a groove, then struck a steel blade set in it. Accounts differ on whether the first blow split the stone or broke the blade. The firm's polishers under Henri Koe worked for months; the firm kept most of the smaller stones as its fee.

sources.title: Royal Collection Trust, 'Mr Asscher using the hammer for the first operation', Feb 1908 (RCIN 2800275)
K. Scarratt and R. Shor, 'The Cullinan Diamond Centennial', Gems & Gemology 42(2), 2006

eyes.name: New Zealand press (Reuters and Press Association cables; Wairarapa Age editorial)
eyes.role: Provincial and city papers printing imperial cables and their own comment
eyes.where: Masterton, Wellington and other New Zealand towns
eyes.vantage_label: the far edge of the Empire, reading cables
eyes.authenticity: Read on Papers Past (National Library of New Zealand): Wairarapa Age 21 Aug 1907 and 13 Nov 1907; Gisborne Times and Rangitikei Advocate 12–13 Nov 1907; Rangitikei Advocate 3 Apr 1908; Dominion 9 Jan 1909. Cable texts were shortened and OCR is imperfect.
eyes.bio: Cables brought each turn of the story to New Zealand within a day or two. One editor saw no loyalty in the gift at all: a poor colony should not give, and a king should not take, a treasure it could not spare.

sources.title: Wairarapa Age, 21 Aug 1907 (Papers Past)
Wairarapa Age, 13 Nov 1907, 'The King and the Diamond'
Dominion, 9 Jan 1909, 'The Cullinan Diamond'

eyes.name: Mothusi Kamanga (with Vuyolwethu Zungula)
eyes.role: Johannesburg lawyer and activist who started an online petition for the stones' return (2022); Zungula is an MP and leader of the African Transformation Movement
eyes.vantage_label: a century on, asking for it back
eyes.authenticity: Positions as reported by AFP (via VOA, 4 May 2023) and Deutsche Welle (via Prothom Alo, 5 May 2023). Modern statements: digested, not quoted.
eyes.bio: After Elizabeth II's death in September 2022, Kamanga's petition asked that the Cullinan stones be returned and shown in a South African museum; it passed 8,000 signatures. Zungula argued that the country's minerals belong to its people and that the stones reached Britain at a human cost. The South African government took no official position.

sources.title: VOA Africa (AFP), 4 May 2023
Prothom Alo (DW), 5 May 2023

entries.date_display: Thursday 26 January 1905 (late afternoon; some sources give 25 January)
entries.headline: A glint high in the pit wall on the evening round
entries.digest: On his routine round of the open pit, Wells saw something shining in the side wall near the rim and dug it out with his pocket-knife. That evening it was weighed and measured in the mine office and word went to the chairman in Johannesburg. His daughter later recalled the scene of sunlight on the pit face.
entries.source_note: Scarratt and Shor (2006) give 26 Jan; Heritage Portal summarises the daughter's 1946 account and the Hatch–Corstorphine pamphlet (25 Jan).

entries.headline: The shift that left no account
entries.digest: The men digging and loading the kimberlite that afternoon were African labourers, but no record consulted names any of them. Helme's 1974 biography of Cullinan says an African worker led Wells to the stone; a modern encyclopedia account instead names a white miner. Guest (2007) calls the finder an unnamed Black labourer. No surviving firsthand account found.
entries.source_note: Guest (2007); Heritage Portal citing Helme (1974). The attribution is disputed and unresolved.

entries.headline: The chairman calls his directors and takes the stone
entries.digest: The morning after the find, Cullinan called a special directors' meeting at his home. Later that day, at the mine, Wells handed the stone to the general manager William McHardy, who passed it to Cullinan, and Cullinan was photographed with it. The stone took his name.
entries.source_note: Heritage Portal (Cullinan Mine Archives; McHardy family accounts). Day depends on whether the find was the 25th or 26th.

entries.headline: Thousands queue at the bank to see the stone
entries.digest: The Leader reported that some 8,000–9,000 people came to view the stone at the Standard Bank, although only about 3,000 passes had been issued. Pride in the find was mixed with regret that a stone so large might be too big to sell. The paper floated a public subscription so that the Empire could buy it for the King.
entries.source_note: Transvaal Leader, 2 Feb 1905, as cited by Scarratt and Shor (2006) and Guest (2007); quote as given by Guest.

entries.place: Geological Society of South Africa, Johannesburg
entries.headline: Measuring a fragment of something larger
entries.digest: Hatch and Corstorphine lectured on the crystal: its dimensions of roughly 10 by 6 by 5 cm, its faces, and the flat cleavage surfaces that suggested it had broken from a bigger stone. The idea of a missing 'other half' started here and was taken up by Molengraaff and later writers.
entries.source_note: Transactions of the Geological Society of South Africa vol. 8 (1906), from a March 1905 lecture (GIA reading list); Guest (2007) on Molengraaff.

entries.headline: A printed description gives the find as 25 January
entries.digest: The pamphlet 'A description of the big diamond recently found in the Premier Mine' set out the measurements and weight for buyers and scientists. It dated the find to 25 January, one day earlier than the company's records. The same text was printed in the Geological Magazine that year.
entries.source_note: Heritage Portal (citing the April 1905 pamphlet); GIA reading list.

entries.headline: The stone goes to the London agents and waits
entries.digest: The company sent the stone to its London sales agents, S. Neumann and Co., valued at about £400,000 and reportedly insured for £500,000. No buyer came forward at that price, and it stayed in a safe for more than two years. Later accounts say it travelled by ordinary registered post while a decoy parcel went under guard by steamer; no contemporary record of the decoy was found.
entries.source_note: Scarratt and Shor (2006) for April 1905 and Neumann; Mining Weekly (2015) for the valuation and posting. Decoy story from later accounts only.

entries.headline: Five hundred men recruited from Nyasaland as an 'experiment'
entries.digest: The Secretary of State for the Colonies sanctioned the recruitment of 500 Nyasaland men for the Premier mine as an experiment. They were brought some 1,500 km south on contracts. No record consulted gives any of their names or words.
entries.source_note: Churchill's answer, Hansard HC Deb 11 Mar 1908.

entries.headline: A return counts 463 Nyasaland men on the mine
entries.digest: A Colonial Office return to the end of July 1907 recorded 463 Nyasaland recruits at work on the Premier mine. Recruiting had stopped after 1906, and the deaths among such men from the tropical north were the stated reason it was not renewed.
entries.source_note: Hansard HC Deb 11 Mar 1908 (return cited by Churchill).

entries.headline: Het Volk caucus backs the gift
entries.digest: Botha won the support of his Het Volk caucus for a motion to buy the stone from the Premier company and present it to the King on behalf of the colony. The colony was in a depression and public servants were being laid off.
entries.source_note: Guest (2007).

entries.headline: Asking the Governor to win over the Opposition
entries.digest: In a private letter Botha asked Selborne to persuade the Progressive leader Sir George Farrar to support the gift, so that it would go to the King as a unanimous act of the colony.
entries.source_note: Botha to Selborne, 15 Aug 1907, Selborne Papers Ms 60 (Bodleian), cited by Guest (2007).

entries.headline: The Governor refuses to lean on the Progressives
entries.digest: Selborne wrote to Farrar that it was not his place to interfere in what the Progressives decided. He kept to the constitutional line while privately hoping the vote would be united.
entries.source_note: Selborne to Farrar, 15 Aug 1907 (copy), Selborne Papers Ms 62, cited by Guest (2007).

entries.headline: Botha moves the gift as a gracious act
entries.digest: Moving the motion, Botha called the purchase a graceful act that would lift the Transvaal above narrow self-interest. He denied any aim to embarrass the Opposition and said no new tax would be raised to pay for it. The motion passed 42 to 19, with Het Volk, the Nationalists and Labour in favour and one Progressive joining them.
entries.source_note: Transvaal Legislative Assembly Debates vol. 1, cols 2505–2508 (19 Aug 1907) and Votes and Proceedings p. 382, cited by Guest (2007); vote confirmed by Reuters cable (Wairarapa Age, 21 Aug 1907).

entries.headline: A Boer general supports the gift but withholds loyalty
entries.digest: De la Rey spoke for the motion, as did his fellow general Beyers, who called it a token from men who had lately been the King's enemies. De la Rey went further in candour: he said he could not yet profess loyalty to the Crown, and that such feeling would come only gradually.
entries.source_note: Assembly Debates cols 2514–2515, cited by Guest (2007).

entries.headline: The Opposition defends its loyalty, quietly
entries.digest: With Farrar's Progressives voting no on grounds of the colony's distress, FitzPatrick rose to defend their motives as loyal. Observers found him unusually subdued. Smuts had already mocked the Opposition and cited Britain's £5 million loan guarantee as cause for gratitude.
entries.source_note: Assembly Debates cols 2516–2520, cited by Guest (2007).

entries.headline: Five private reasons for voting no
entries.digest: Writing to his son, FitzPatrick listed five reasons the Progressives opposed the gift. Among them: that it was a bribe aimed at British opinion while the loan was before Parliament, and a party manoeuvre that used the King's name to force their hand.
entries.source_note: FitzPatrick to N. FitzPatrick, 20 Aug 1907, NELM FitzPatrick Papers A/L 4, cited by Guest (2007).

entries.headline: Advising the King how to read the vote
entries.digest: Selborne sent the King's secretary Lord Knollys his view: Botha meant the gift as a sign that Afrikaners accepted British rule, and the Progressive minority had voted from a sincere, if mistaken, sense of duty that deserved recognition.
entries.source_note: Selborne to Knollys, 20 Aug 1907 (copy), Selborne Papers Ms 54, cited by Guest (2007).

entries.date_display: Wednesday 21 August 1907 (cable from London of 20 Aug)
entries.headline: Cable: Assembly votes 42 to 19 for the gift
entries.digest: A Reuters cable from Pretoria reached New Zealand within two days. It reported Botha's plea for unanimity and his promise of no new tax, Farrar's regretful dissent on the ground of distress among loyal subjects, and Labour's support.
entries.source_note: Wairarapa Age, 21 Aug 1907, p. 5 (Papers Past).

entries.headline: Telegram to Churchill at the Colonial Office
entries.digest: Selborne cabled Churchill privately about the gift, pressing the case for acceptance in London. A formal despatch to the Secretary of State, Lord Elgin, followed on 26 August.
entries.source_note: Selborne to Churchill, telegram, 22 Aug 1907, Selborne Papers Ms 70; Selborne to Elgin, 26 Aug 1907, CO 879/94; both cited by Guest (2007).

entries.headline: The owner sits in the Assembly that buys his stone
entries.digest: Cullinan, member for Pretoria North-West, was a friend of Botha and Smuts and linked by marriage to E. P. Solomon. Guest suggests such ties help explain why the Progressives did not attack the company itself in the debate. The colony paid £150,000; Mining Weekly puts the net cost at about £60,000 once the state's share of the mine's profits is deducted.
entries.source_note: Guest (2007); Scarratt and Shor (2006) on the £150,000 price and the 60% profits tax; Mining Weekly (2015) on the net cost.

entries.headline: The King, on Cabinet advice, will accept
entries.digest: Knollys wrote to Selborne that the King would accept the stone. He would do so as an expression of loyalty from the whole colony irrespective of party, without the praise for the opponents' motives that Selborne had suggested.
entries.source_note: Knollys to Selborne, 20 Sep 1907, Selborne Papers Ms 54/70, cited by Guest (2007).

entries.place: Letter from Barbon Manor, Kirkby Lonsdale, to Churchill
entries.headline: Hopwood reports the King's agreement
entries.digest: Sir Francis Hopwood, Permanent Under-Secretary at the Colonial Office, wrote to Churchill on a mix of colonial business: a quarrel with Newfoundland's premier, Natal's government, and the King's agreement to accept the Cullinan Diamond. The letter sits among Churchill's official papers for 1907.
entries.source_note: Churchill Archives Centre, CHAR 2/30/84.

entries.headline: The stone is handed to the King at Sandringham
entries.digest: Sir Richard Solomon, Agent-General for the Transvaal, presented the rough stone to the King at Sandringham on his birthday. Later accounts add that he came by train with Hopwood and Scotland Yard detectives, before a party of royal guests.
entries.source_note: Press Association cable, London 10 Nov 1907 (Gisborne Times 13 Nov 1907; Rangitikei Advocate 12 Nov 1907); RCT 31712 for date and place. Escort details from later accounts.

entries.headline: The acceptance cabled to the Transvaal ministry
entries.digest: The King had Lord Elgin cable Botha's ministry that he accepted the stone as a sign of the Transvaal people's loyalty to his throne and person. He would keep it among the Crown's heirlooms, and he thanked the ministry for its birthday congratulations.
entries.quote: token of the loyalty and attachment of the people of the Transvaal
entries.source_note: Press Association cable, London 11 Nov 1907, printed in Gisborne Times 13 Nov 1907 (Papers Past).

entries.headline: An editor calls the whole affair a mistake
entries.digest: The Wairarapa Age argued that the King should not have taken, nor a depressed colony given, a treasure it could ill afford. It doubted the loyalty of the Boer government and suggested the King would have done better to return a share of the value to the Transvaal.
entries.quote: There is something about the whole proceeding that is incomprehensible.
entries.source_note: Wairarapa Age, 13 Nov 1907, p. 4, 'The King and the Diamond' (Papers Past).

entries.headline: An agreement for inspecting the cutting
entries.digest: The King's representatives signed an agreement with the London brokers M. J. Levy and Nephews, who were to act as inspectors over the stone while Asscher's firm cut it. It set out how the stone was to be handled and each party's duties.
entries.source_note: National Jeweler (24 Apr 2019) on the Bonhams lot 'Agreement for the Inspection of the Cullinan Diamond'; Dominion, 9 Jan 1909, on Levy as inspectors.

entries.headline: Studying the stone and its two flaws
entries.digest: Joseph Asscher began his examination of the rough, which had two visible inclusions that would decide where it must be split. The firm's directors, some brought from Paris, spent about a fortnight agreeing on the line of the cleave.
entries.source_note: Scarratt and Shor (2006) for the date; Dominion, 9 Jan 1909, and Frankfurter Zeitung report reprinted in a Nebraska German-language paper, 6 Mar 1908, on the deliberations.

entries.headline: The blow: a blade breaks, a stone splits
entries.digest: After cutting a groove with sharp diamond splinters over several days, Asscher set a specially made steel blade in it and struck it with a heavy steel rod. In the account most often told, the first blow broke the blade and a second split the stone. A cable dated the next day reported the cleaving as a success, giving pieces of about 1,977 and 1,040 Dutch carats.
entries.source_note: Scarratt and Shor (2006); press cable London 11 Feb 1908 (Rangitikei Advocate, 3 Apr 1908). Order of events differs between sources.

entries.headline: 'The King's diamond' cleft in Amsterdam
entries.digest: The cable described the stone set in cement, the groove cut with the sharpest diamonds, the steel blade and the single blow. It added that Henri Koe would polish it in a locked room with three assistants, and that the head of the firm locked it in the safe each night, armed with a revolver.
entries.source_note: Rangitikei Advocate, 3 Apr 1908, p. 7 (London, 11 Feb).

entries.headline: The larger half split again
entries.digest: The larger piece was cleft again in a more delicate operation, with two assistants holding the blade instead of one hand. The blade broke after this final split. Later legend says Asscher fainted at the first blow; his nephew Louis said no Asscher would ever faint over a diamond.
entries.source_note: Scarratt and Shor (2006); Dominion, 9 Jan 1909. Fainting story: later legend, denied by the family (Royal Asscher account).

entries.headline: Henri Koe begins polishing the great drop
entries.digest: Polishing of the piece that became Cullinan I began under the chief polisher Henri Koe, on a wheel turning about 2,400 times a minute in a felt-floored room on the factory's third floor. Polishers there earned some 40 to 50 guilders a week, often for only part of the year.
entries.source_note: Scarratt and Shor (2006); Dominion, 9 Jan 1909; Frankfurter Zeitung report reprinted 6 Mar 1908.

entries.headline: Questions in the Commons about the Premier mine's recruits
entries.digest: Asked how many Central Africans worked on the Premier mine, Churchill gave the return of 463 Nyasaland men and said resuming recruitment had been refused because the mortality did not justify it. A question on whether the men were separated from their wives in near-servile conditions went unanswered.
entries.quote: cannot be authorised in existing circumstances
entries.source_note: Hansard HC Deb 11 Mar 1908 vol 185 cc1517–9.

entries.headline: Work begins on the second great stone
entries.digest: Polishers started on the section that became Cullinan II, a cushion-shaped brilliant. The work ran in long shifts under guard.
entries.source_note: Scarratt and Shor (2006).

entries.headline: Cullinan I finished: 530.2 carats, 74 facets
entries.digest: The great pear-shaped drop was completed at 530.2 metric carats with 74 facets, more than the usual 58. All the stones were done by early November: nine major gems, 96 small brilliants and about nine carats of unpolished fragments.
entries.source_note: Scarratt and Shor (2006); Guest (2007); Dominion, 9 Jan 1909.

entries.headline: The King receives the two Stars
entries.digest: Cullinan I and Cullinan II were presented to the King at Windsor. The rest of the major stones went to the Asscher firm as its fee, apart from one the King bought for Queen Alexandra.
entries.source_note: Scarratt and Shor (2006); Guest (2007).

entries.headline: A full account of the cutting reaches the Dominion
entries.digest: The Wellington paper summarised the story from find to finish: Wells's evening round, the stone's weight of about 3,025 carats, the fortnight of planning, the two cleavings and the felt-floored grinding room. It gave the largest stone as 510¾ carats in the old reckoning, roughly five times the Koh-i-Noor.
entries.source_note: Dominion, 9 Jan 1909, p. 10 (Papers Past; OCR, figures in old carats).

entries.headline: Cullinan II set in the Imperial State Crown
entries.digest: The 317.4-carat Cullinan II was set at the front of the Imperial State Crown's band, pushing the Stuart Sapphire to the back.
entries.source_note: Royal Collection Trust, RCIN 31701.

entries.date_display: 1910 (after the accession of George V, 6 May)
entries.headline: The Great Star goes into the Sceptre
entries.digest: The Sovereign's Sceptre with Cross, made for Charles II in 1661, was altered to hold Cullinan I. In the same year six of the stones kept by Asscher were bought and presented to Queen Mary on behalf of the people of South Africa.
entries.source_note: Royal Collection Trust, RCIN 31712; Guest (2007); Scarratt and Shor (2006).

entries.headline: Two more Cullinans crown a queen
entries.digest: Cullinan III and IV were set in a detachable mount in the crown made for Queen Mary's coronation; she later had them replaced by replicas.
entries.source_note: Scarratt and Shor (2006).

entries.headline: A petition after the Queen's death
entries.digest: After Elizabeth II died, Kamanga started an online petition asking the new King to return the Cullinan stones and show them in a South African museum. He argued that decolonisation meant reclaiming property as well as winning freedoms. It passed 8,000 signatures.
entries.source_note: Deutsche Welle via Prothom Alo, 5 May 2023; AFP via VOA, 4 May 2023. Exact launch date not confirmed.

entries.headline: Before a coronation, a demand that the stones come home
entries.digest: Speaking to AFP before Charles III's coronation, Zungula said the country's minerals belonged to its people, not to the British palace, and that lives had been lost to bring the diamonds to Britain. Neither the South African government nor the palace gave an official response.
entries.source_note: VOA Africa (AFP), 4 May 2023.

claims.claim: Date of the find given as 25 January 1905, one day before the company's date: a position, not settled.
claims.evidence: Hatch and Corstorphine pamphlet, April 1905 (cited by the Heritage Portal)

claims.claim: Rough diamond of 3,025¾ carats (period English carats; about 3,106 metric carats, 621 g), c. 10 × 6 × 5 cm, taken from the Premier pit wall.
claims.evidence: Company records via Scarratt and Shor (2006); Guest (2007); press cables 1907

claims.claim: Finder: credited to Wells; Helme (1974) says an African worker led him to the stone; another account names a white miner. No worker is named in any record consulted.
About 8,000–9,000 visitors at the Standard Bank display against roughly 3,000 passes issued.
claims.evidence: Transvaal Leader, 2 Feb 1905, cited by Scarratt and Shor (2006)

claims.claim: Stone sent to S. Neumann & Co., London; valued about £400,000, insured £500,000; unsold for over two years. Decoy-steamer and ordinary-parcel-post story: later accounts only, unsupported by any contemporary record found.
463 Nyasaland recruits on the Premier mine (of 500 sanctioned in November 1906); recruiting not renewed because of mortality.
claims.evidence: Colonial Office return cited in Hansard, HC Deb 11 Mar 1908

claims.claim: Assembly motion to buy the stone for £150,000 and present it to the King carried 42 to 19 (Het Volk, National, Labour and one Progressive in favour; Progressives against).
claims.evidence: Transvaal Legislative Assembly Debates vol. 1 cols 2505–2520; Votes and Proceedings p. 382 (via Guest 2007); Reuters cable 20 Aug 1907

claims.claim: Legislative Council defeated, 7 to 5, a motion that the stone be bought by public subscription rather than public funds; votes largely on language lines.
Progressive position: the gift was a bribe to British opinion during the £5 million loan debate and a party move using the King's name.
claims.evidence: FitzPatrick to his son, NELM A/L 4 (via Guest 2007)

claims.claim: Rough stone presented to Edward VII at Sandringham on his 66th birthday; accepted, to be kept among the Crown heirlooms, as a token of the colony's loyalty.
claims.evidence: Press Association cables 10–11 Nov 1907; CO 879/106 p. 173 (via Guest 2007); RCT 31712

claims.claim: First cleaving: pieces of 1,977½ and 1,040½ Dutch carats (2,029.9 and 1,068.8 metric). Sources differ on whether the first blow split the stone or broke the blade; the fainting story is legend.
claims.evidence: Scarratt and Shor (2006); cable of 11 Feb 1908; Dominion 9 Jan 1909

claims.claim: Yield: 9 major stones (Cullinan I 530.2 ct, II 317.4, III 94.4, IV 63.6, V 18.8, VI 11.5, VII 8.8, VIII 6.8, IX 4.39), 96 small brilliants, about 9 ct of fragments.
Cullinan I and II delivered to the King at Windsor; the other seven major stones retained by Asscher as fee (one later bought for Queen Alexandra).
Cullinan II (317.4 ct) set in the front of the Imperial State Crown.
Cullinan I (530.2 ct) set in the Sovereign's Sceptre with Cross; six stones presented to Queen Mary on behalf of the people of South Africa.

Restitution position: an online petition of more than 8,000 signatures asks for the stones' return; the opposing position is that the stone was bought and given by the colony's elected government. No government has taken an official stance.
claims.evidence: AFP via VOA (4 May 2023); DW via Prothom Alo (5 May 2023); Guest (2007) on the 1907 purchase

convergences.label: The find at the Premier mine
convergences.note: The manager's story, the chairman's name and the silence of the shift: the record credits Wells, names the stone for Cullinan, and leaves the African worker who in some accounts spotted it without a name.

convergences.label: The stone on show and on paper
convergences.note: Within weeks the crowd at the bank, the geologists' measurements and the company's sales plan each turned the same crystal into a different object: a spectacle, a specimen, an unsellable asset.

convergences.label: The Assembly votes 42 to 19
convergences.note: Botha speaks of a gracious act, De la Rey supports it while refusing to claim loyalty, FitzPatrick defends a 'no' as loyal, and a cable carries Farrar's 'inopportune and unjustifiable' to the far side of the world.

convergences.label: Private letters the day after
convergences.note: FitzPatrick tells his son it is a bribe; Selborne tells the Palace it is a sign of Afrikaner acceptance and asks that the minority be honoured; within two days he cables Churchill.

convergences.label: Sandringham and the reaction
convergences.note: The King takes the stone as loyalty from the whole colony; a New Zealand editor calls the affair incomprehensible; Churchill's file already holds the news of acceptance.

convergences.label: The cleaving in Amsterdam
convergences.note: The cutter's blow, the cable's tidy version of it, and the inspectors working for the King under the January agreement: three accounts that do not agree on which blow did the work.

convergences.label: Polishing and the Commons question
convergences.note: The week the polishing of Cullinan I was under way, Churchill told the Commons that recruiting for the same mine had been stopped because too many of the men died.

convergences.label: A coronation and a claim
convergences.note: The stones set in 1909–10 return to the news before Charles III's coronation, as campaigners argue the gift of 1907 was never the people's to give.

ties.note: Wells's find passed via the general manager McHardy to Cullinan the next day; the stone took the chairman's name, not the finder's.
Wells supervised the pit where the African workforce dug; some accounts say one of them showed him the stone.
Hatch and Corstorphine's description of Wells's stone gave the find a date one day earlier than the company's.
Comrades in the Boer War and in Het Volk; De la Rey backed Botha's motion while openly withholding the loyalty Botha's gift implied.
Botha asked Selborne by letter to win over the Opposition; Selborne declined and then argued Botha's case to the Palace.
Botha's motion and FitzPatrick's 'no' in the same debate; each claimed loyalty to the Crown.
Selborne's private telegram of 22 August 1907 went to Churchill at the Colonial Office.
Churchill answered for the Nyasaland recruits on the Premier mine in the Commons in March 1908.
Cullinan engaged the Asscher firm for the cutting before the colony bought the stone.
Asscher cut the King's stone under inspectors appointed for him; Cullinan I and II were delivered at Windsor.
The Leader first proposed in 1905 that the Empire buy the stone for the King; the colony's government did so in 1907.
The Wairarapa Age doubted the loyalty behind Botha's gift.
The restitution campaigners ask the Crown that has held the stones since 1907 to return them.

threads_out.note: Guest notes the Cullinan was about thirty-six times larger than the stone that set off the Griqualand West rush of 1869. The Premier's labour system and its rivalry with De Beers grew out of the Kimberley diamond fields.
The Progressives who opposed the gift in 1907, Farrar and FitzPatrick, and the financier Julius Wernher who called it a clever move, were leading figures of the Rand gold-mining houses.
Both stones became British crown jewels, and both now face calls for return. Cullinan III and IV were set in Queen Mary's 1911 crown, the same crown that carried the Koh-i-Noor.

Botha led South Africa into the First World War in 1914. De la Rey, who spoke on the gift in 1907, was shot dead at a police roadblock in September 1914 on the eve of the Afrikaner rebellion against that decision.

images.title: Cullinan Diamond: models of the original stone
images.caption: Platinum print of two models of the rough stone, from the Asscher firm's album acquired by George V. The rough itself was destroyed in cutting; models are how its shape survives.
images.credit: Unknown photographer; Royal Collection Trust, RCIN 2800269

images.title: Mr Asscher using the hammer for the first operation on the Cullinan Diamond
images.caption: Joseph Asscher strikes the blade set in the stone, held in a vice. Probably a posed record of the operation for the firm's album, not a snapshot of the moment.
images.credit: Joseph Asscher & Cie album; Royal Collection Trust, RCIN 2800275

images.title: Cullinan Diamond: cleaving of the second largest portion and the final seven pieces
images.caption: Top: the second-largest portion after it was split. Bottom: the seven pieces cut from the original stone, largest to smallest.
images.credit: Joseph Asscher & Cie album; Royal Collection Trust, RCIN 2800271

images.title: The Sovereign's Sceptre with Cross
images.caption: Made for Charles II in 1661 and altered in 1910 to hold Cullinan I (530.2 carats).

images.title: The Imperial State Crown
images.caption: Made for George VI in 1937. Cullinan II (317.4 carats) has been at the front of the band since 1909, moved from the earlier crown.

images.title: Queen Mary's Crown
images.caption: Made for Queen Mary's coronation in 1911. It originally held Cullinan III and IV in a detachable setting, later replaced by replicas.
